planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated transplants in spring in well-drained, unimproved prairie soil in full sun; Mead's milkweed is federally threatened, so source only from reputable native plant nurseries propagating stock legally, never from wild-collected plants.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated transplants in spring in well-drained, unimproved prairie soil in full sun; Mead's milkweed is federally threatened, so source only from reputable native plant nurseries propagating stock legally, never from wild-collected plants. Slender, upright stems bear pairs of broad leaves and a single nodding cluster of pale greenish-white, waxy flowers in early summer, a subdued flower display compared to showier milkweed relatives but no less valuable as a monarch butterfly host plant and native pollinator resource. Once widespread across unplowed tallgrass prairie remnants of the central United States, habitat loss from prairie conversion to agriculture has made it federally listed as threatened, and it survives today mostly in scattered high-quality prairie remnants and conservation plantings. Growing it in a home native prairie garden from responsibly sourced nursery stock helps support genetic diversity and public awareness of this declining prairie specialist, which needs undisturbed, unimproved soil and years of patient establishment before reliably flowering.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; pineland milkweed is adapted to fire-maintained sandy pinelands and needs sharp drainage.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; pineland milkweed is adapted to fire-maintained sandy pinelands and needs sharp drainage. Softly hairy, oval, gray-green leaves and rounded clusters of small, dull greenish-white to pale yellow flowers give this milkweed a subtler, more muted appearance than the bright orange or pink of showier relatives, but it serves the same essential role as a monarch butterfly larval host plant across the sandy pine woodlands of the southeastern and Gulf coastal plain. Native to fire-adapted longleaf pine sandhills and open sandy woods, it tolerates the dry, nutrient-poor, well-drained soils typical of that ecosystem and benefits from occasional disturbance or periodic burning in a restoration context, though a home garden planting simply needs sharp drainage and full to partial sun. It requires no supplemental water or fertilizer once established in appropriately lean, sandy soil.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; devil's claw sprawls widely and needs plenty of room, and its sticky, glandular foliage can irritate sensitive skin.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; devil's claw sprawls widely and needs plenty of room, and its sticky, glandular foliage can irritate sensitive skin. Large, sprawling, sticky-hairy leaves and showy, orchid-like, pale pink to lavender flowers give way to the plant's real claim to fame: long, curved, green seed pods that, when young and tender, are pickled or cooked like okra, and when mature dry to a woody, split, two-pronged 'claw' historically gathered by Indigenous peoples of the Southwest and used as a black fiber in basketry. Native to the central and southwestern United States, it grows easily from seed in ordinary garden soil and self-sows readily once established, sometimes appearing as a volunteer weed in disturbed garden soil in following years. Harvest pods young and tender (a few inches long) for pickling and eating, or let some mature and dry fully on the plant to collect the distinctive woody claws for craft use or seed saving.
sources: Slow Food International Ark of Taste
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; maroon blanketflower is drought-tolerant once established and self-sows readily in favorable sandy or gravelly soil.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; maroon blanketflower is drought-tolerant once established and self-sows readily in favorable sandy or gravelly soil. Unlike the familiar red-and-yellow bicolor blanket flower, this Texas native produces entirely solid, deep wine-red to maroon daisy-like flowers with no yellow at all, a rich, unusual monochromatic color unique among commonly grown gaillardia species, blooming through summer on wiry, branching stems. Native to sandy prairies and open ground across central and south Texas, it tolerates heat and drought with ease once established and provides a striking, deep color accent for a native wildflower meadow or xeriscape planting alongside its more common orange-and-yellow relatives. It self-sows readily in loose, well-drained soil and needs no supplemental water or fertilizer once established.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Mahogany plains coreopsis self-sows readily and naturalizes into drifts in favorable meadow or wildflower plantings.

directions: Direct sow in early spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Mahogany plains coreopsis self-sows readily and naturalizes into drifts in favorable meadow or wildflower plantings. This selection of the widespread native plains coreopsis produces small, solid, deep mahogany-red flowers with no yellow banding, a richer, more uniform color than the classic red-and-yellow bicolor form of the wild species, blooming prolifically on airy, finely branched stems from summer through fall. Extremely easy from seed and adaptable to a wide range of soils and climates, it is a staple of native wildflower meadow mixes across North America, providing abundant nectar and pollen for a wide range of small native bees and other pollinators. It self-sows readily once established, requiring no fertilizer or supplemental water, and is best massed in a meadow or informal border where its airy, branching form can be appreciated in drifts.
